land.text: the Tây Sơn lands, taken from Saigon in 1788 to Hanoi in July 1802

predecessors.note: Nguyễn Ánh recaptured Gia Định on 7 September 1788 and Hanoi in July 1802, ending the Tây Sơn dynasty (the Tây Sơn page gives 18 June 1802).

land.text: the southern realm of the Nguyễn lords, whose rule dates from 1558

predecessors.note: The same house: Nguyễn Ánh was the Nguyễn lords' surviving heir; Cliopatria draws the Nguyễn lords to 1775 and the dynasty from 1791.

land.text: Annam and Tonkin as French protectorates (the Treaty of Patenôtre (6 June 1884) ... creating the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin), with Cochinchina already French since 1862-1867

successors.note: The Nguyễn emperors reigned on as figureheads until 25 August 1945; the sovereign state of this dossier ends with the protectorate. Cliopatria's last Nguyễn shape is 1884.

capitals.name: Gia Định (Saigon)
capitals.note: Saigon captured on 7 September 1788; 30,000 people mobilised in 1790 to build the Saigon citadel.

capitals.name: Huế (Phú Xuân)
capitals.note: Phú Xuân was seized on 3 May 1801 and Gia Long was crowned at Huế on 1 June 1802.

rulers.name: Nguyễn Ánh (Gia Long)
rulers.note: Lord in the south from 1788, emperor from 1 June 1802; the page gives his reign as 1802 until his death in 1819.

rulers.name: Tự Đức
rulers.note: The page gives 1847/1848 for the start.

rulers.name: Dục Đức
rulers.note: Deposed and executed after three days.

rulers.name: Kiến Phúc
rulers.note: The page says only from late 1883; the end year is not given.

correction.text: Gia Định (Saigon), Mỹ Tho and the southern delta around them, as Cliopatria's 1791 shape

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Nguyễn shape begins in 1791, but 'his soldiers captured Saigon on 7 September 1788' and Mỹ Tho became the main staging point. The 1788-1790 extent is taken to be the 1791 shape; the pages give no boundary.

8,428 km2 (24 cells) in the Saigon-Mỹ Tho delta: unverified for extent. The pages say only that the combined forces 'consolidated Nguyễn Phúc Ánh's hold on southern Vietnam' (1789) and that a citadel was built at Saigon in 1790. The shape is far smaller than the Mekong delta the French took in 1859-1867 (215 cells), so it may undercount; a gap-filler should open a page on the Gia Định régime. The Nguyen page gives no area figure to compare.

17,864 km2: the 1791 shape plus 13 Khánh Hòa cells and 15 Đắk Lắk cells. 'In 1794, after a successful campaign in the Nha Trang region', Nguyễn Phúc Ánh ordered a citadel built at Duyên Khánh; the Tây Sơn besieged it in May 1794 without success.

33,901 km2: adds Phú Yên and highland cells (18 Phú Yên, 7 Gia Lai, 27 Đắk Lắk). Unverified: neither the Gia Long nor the Tây Sơn page dates the advance to Phú Yên; the Gia Long page has fighting at Thi Nai in 1792-1793 and at Qui Nhơn in 1799.

36,047 km2: adds 5 Bình Định cells. 'Heavy fighting occurred at the fortress of Qui Nhơn until it was captured in 1799 by Nguyen Canh's forces.' The city 'was quickly lost and was not regained until 1801'.

correction.text: the shape unchanged, valid for 1800 only; the new 1801 keyframe carries 1801-1802

keyframe_review.note: 33,901 km2, the 1796 shape again: Quy Nhơn lost. The shape holds for 1800 only: in 1801 the Nguyễn took Qui Nhơn ('not regained until 1801') and Phú Xuân on 3 May 1801 (Nguyen page); the Tây Sơn page says 'In 1800, Nguyễn Ánh occupied Quy Nhơn citadel', one year earlier than the Gia Long page.

union.text: the Tây Sơn heartland between Quy Nhơn and Phú Xuân (Huế)

correction.text: the 1800 shape plus the central coast from Quy Nhơn to Phú Xuân, taken in 1801

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1801-1802: Cliopatria keeps the 1800 shape until 1802 although Nguyễn Ánh seized the capital, Phú Xuân on 3 May 1801 and Qui Nhơn was regained in 1801. The north (Tây Sơn rump at Bắc Thành) falls on 20 July 1802, when the ledger adds it.

296,698 km2: the whole of Vietnam, Tonkin to Cà Mau. Ánh captured Hanoi (Thăng Long) on 20 July 1802 (the Gia Long page says 22 July, the Tây Sơn infobox 18 June). The Nguyen page gives no area. The outline carries 7 Chinese, 6 Cambodian and 1 Lao cell at the margin, which is coarse outline, not a claim.

300,553 km2: +12 cells (Ninh Thuận 11, Đông Nam Bộ 11) over 1803. Unverified: none of the five pages opened mentions the Cham principality of Panduranga or an annexation of 1832-1834. The ledger records the gain in November 1832 (Champa page, added by reviewer se-01-j); Cliopatria draws it from 1834.

correction.text: the 1859 shape plus Cochinchina, which the Nguyễn held until the treaty of June 1862 (eastern provinces) and 1867 (western provinces)

keyframe_review.note: 234,164 km2: Cliopatria takes the whole Mekong delta (215 cells) out of the Nguyễn shape in 1859 and gives it to French Indochina from 1860. The page dates it in steps: Saigon captured in early 1859 (17 February), in June 1862, the Treaty of Saigon ceded Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa, and in 1867 the French annexed Vĩnh Long, Hà Tiên and Châu Đốc ... without resistance. The corrected 1859 shape keeps the delta; the ledger removes it in 1862 and 1867.

234,652 km2: the Nguyễn state without Cochinchina after the annexation of the western provinces in 1867; the 1874 Treaty of Saigon concluded the French annexation of Cochinchina without moving the line.
234,420 km2: no territorial change on the pages opened (1874 treaty, 1863 Treaty of Huế that increased French control over foreign affairs).

234,420 km2: the shape Cliopatria keeps to 1884. The Harmand Convention (August or September 1883) turned Northern Vietnam into a French protectorate and the Treaty of Patenôtre of 6 June 1884 created the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin, so sovereignty ends in 1883-1884; the ledger carries both steps.

region.text: Gia Định (Saigon) and Mỹ Tho in the southern delta

ledger.note: 1788: Nguyễn Ánh retakes Saigon and founds his southern state. 'After a hard-fought battle, his soldiers captured Saigon on 7 September 1788'; the Nguyen page dates the recapture to 1787 in one passage and 1788 in another, and the Tây Sơn page adds that Nguyễn Lữ's territory was captured by Nguyễn Ánh in 1789. The pages give the town, not a boundary: the core is Cliopatria's 1791 shape.

region.text: the Nha Trang-Khánh Hòa coast and the highlands behind it, added in Cliopatria's 1794 shape

ledger.note: 1794: the Nguyễn take Nha Trang and Khánh Hòa. 'In 1794, after a successful campaign in the Nha Trang region', Nguyễn Phúc Ánh ordered a citadel built at Duyên Khánh; 'The Tây Sơn laid siege to Duyen Khanh in May 1794, but Nguyen forces were able to keep them out.'

region.text: Phú Yên, Gia Lai and Đắk Lắk cells added in Cliopatria's 1796 shape

ledger.note: 1796: Cliopatria extends the Nguyễn shape to Phú Yên and the highlands behind it (about 55 cells). The pages opened date no campaign there, so this is a gap, not a finding.

region.text: the Qui Nhơn area in Bình Định

ledger.note: 1799: Qui Nhơn falls to the Nguyễn. 'Heavy fighting occurred at the fortress of Qui Nhơn until it was captured in 1799 by Nguyen Canh's forces.'

region.text: the Qui Nhơn area in Bình Định

ledger.note: 1800: Qui Nhơn is lost again: 'the city was quickly lost and was not regained until 1801.' The page gives no year for the loss; Cliopatria's 1800 shape drops it. The Tây Sơn page says 'In 1800, Nguyễn Ánh occupied Quy Nhơn citadel', so the two pages disagree by a year.

region.text: the Tây Sơn heartland between Quy Nhơn and Phú Xuân (Huế)

ledger.note: 1801: the Nguyễn seize Qui Nhơn and the capital. On 3 May 1801, Nguyễn Ánh seized the capital, Phú Xuân (Nguyen page); Qui Nhơn was 'not regained until 1801' (Gia Long page). The Tây Sơn page confirms 'In 1801, he occupied Phú Xuân'. The land between is the researcher's reading.
1802: Nguyễn Ánh is crowned Emperor Gia Long at Huế. 'Gia Long's coronation: celebrated his coronation at Huế on 1 June 1802.' The Nguyễn lord becomes emperor; colour and dossier continue.
1802: the court is at Huế (Phú Xuân), seized in 1801; the Gia Định citadel (Saigon) was the seat from 1788.

union.text: the Tây Sơn heartland between Quy Nhơn and Phú Xuân (Huế)

minus.text: the 1800 shape plus the central coast from Quy Nhơn to Phú Xuân, taken in 1801

region.text: the rest of Vietnam north of Huế, Thanh Hóa, Nghệ An and Tonkin, the Tây Sơn rump at Bắc Thành

ledger.note: 1802: Hanoi falls and the Tây Sơn end. On 20 July 1802, Ánh captured Hanoi (Thăng Long), ending the Tây Sơn dynasty. The Gia Long page gives 22 July, the Tây Sơn infobox 18 June; the Tây Sơn heir Nguyễn Quang Toản was captured and executed.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1803: Cambodia becomes a Vietnamese vassal. Gia Long expelled Siamese forces from Cambodia 'turning it into a vassal state'; 'in 1803, a Cambodian mission paid tribute to Vietnam', then annually; in 1807 Ang Chan asked for formal investiture, and in 1813 a Vietnamese garrison was installed at Phnom Penh.

region.text: Savannakhet and Xam Neua (Houaphan)

ledger.note: 1827: Vietnam seizes Savannakhet and Xam Neua. Minh Mạng backed the revolt of King Anouvong of Vientiane, and seized Xam Neua and Savannakhet in 1827. The Siamese-Vietnamese War page records Siam's annexation of Vientiane's lands in 1828.

region.text: Savannakhet and Xam Neua (Houaphan)

ledger.note: 1828: the Vietnamese hold on Savannakhet and Xam Neua ends no later than the Siamese annexation of Vientiane's lands (Cliopatria's 1828 Siam shape holds Savannakhet). The page gives no end date: a gap.

region.text: the last remnants of Champa (Panduranga), incorporated into the Ninh Thuan and Binh Thuan provinces: the cells Cliopatria adds in its 1834 shape

ledger.note: 1832: Minh Mạng annexes Panduranga, the last Cham principality. Champa infobox: 'Panduranga annexed by Vietnam under Nguyễn dynasty: November 1832'; the text has Panduranga surviving until August 1832, when Minh Mạng began his purge, incorporating the last remnants of Champa into the Ninh Thuận and Bình Thuận provinces. Cliopatria adds the cells only in its 1834 shape. [Reviewer se-01-j, 2026-10-19: re-dated from 1834 (confidence 1, no page) to November 1832 on the Champa page, matching the champa dossier's 1832 dissolve.]

region.text: Saigon and its citadel

ledger.note: 1833: the Lê Văn Khôi revolt takes Saigon. 'Lê Văn Khôi, adopted son of Lê Văn Duyệt, arose in rebellion against Minh Mạng in April 1833'; the rebels seized Saigon and were reduced to the Saigon citadel by late 1833. The rebels are not a Cliopatria row.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1833: Siam invades Cambodia and Hà Tiên. Siamese forces left Bangkok on November 23, 1833; the Siamese took Hà Tiên in January 1834 and were beaten at Vàm Nao on 21 January 1834.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1834: Minh Mạng ends Cambodia's vassalage: he 'declared full suzerainty over Cambodia, which he demoted to Vietnam's 32nd province'; the Nguyen page: Minh Mạng fully annexed Cambodia and renamed it Tây Thành Province.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1834: the Siamese are driven out. By April 1834 they had all withdrawn; Vietnamese and Cambodian forces controlled Pursat.

region.text: Saigon and its citadel

ledger.note: 1835: Saigon is recaptured from Lê Văn Khôi's rebels: Saigon was recaptured in September 1835 (Khôi died in December 1834).

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1835: Vietnam organises eastern Cambodia as Trấn Tây Province. Vietnam set up Trấn Tây Province in November 1835, with Trương Minh Giảng as Governor-General. Saigon is also recaptured from the rebels in September 1835.

1839: the official name becomes Đại Nam. In 1839, the official name became Đại Việt Nam, shortened to Đại Nam; the name Việt Nam had been used officially from 1804 to 1813 (Gia Long page: Jiaqing 'agreed to change it to Việt Nam').

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1841: Siam aids the Khmer revolt against Vietnamese rule. 'In 1841, Siam seized the opportunity of discontent to aid the Khmer revolt against Vietnamese rule'; the Vietnamese won at Châu Đốc on 8 April 1842 and took Phnom Penh on 11 September 1845.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1847: agreement on Cambodia. 'Only after the Vietnamese had sent an ultimatum in October 1846 was an agreement finally reached in January 1847.'

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1847: Vietnam withdraws from Cambodia: 'The Vietnamese withdrew their forces from Cambodia in mid-1847 and Siam did the same in April 1848.' Ang Duong sent a mission to Huế and was invested in May 1847.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1847: Cambodia is again a Vietnamese tributary, under joint suzerainty. 'Cambodia came under joint Siamese-Vietnamese suzerainty'; 'tributes would be submitted to both courts at Bangkok and Huế'; Huế invested Ang Duong in May 1847; the relation takes effect when the Vietnamese leave in mid-1847.

region.text: Đà Nẵng, where the Franco-Spanish force landed

ledger.note: 1858: the French landing at Đà Nẵng opens the Cochinchina campaign: In September 1858, the Franco-Spanish force invaded Đà Nẵng.

region.text: Saigon and its citadel

ledger.note: 1859: the French take Saigon: The alliance captured Saigon in early 1859 (caption: 17 February 1859). The Nguyễn kept the provinces around it until 1862.

region.text: Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa, the three eastern provinces of Cochinchina (modern Ho Chi Minh City, Long An, Tây Ninh, Bình Dương, Đồng Nai, Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu, Tiền Giang)

ledger.note: 1862: the Treaty of Saigon cedes the three eastern provinces. On June 1862, the Treaty of Saigon ceded Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa, which became French Cochinchina. (The 1863 Treaty of Huế then opened ports and gave France control over foreign affairs.)

region.text: Saigon and its citadel

ledger.note: 1862: the French occupation of Saigon becomes annexation with the treaty of June 1862.

region.text: Đà Nẵng

ledger.note: 1862: the Cochinchina campaign ends with the Treaty of Saigon of June 1862; the Đà Nẵng front is not dated by the page.

region.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

ledger.note: 1863: Cambodia leaves Huế's suzerainty in practice when France places it under protection (the Rattanakosin Kingdom page: France placed Cambodia under protection in 1863). The Nguyen page does not mention Cambodia after 1834; the year is a bridging judgment.

minus.text: Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa, the three eastern provinces of Cochinchina (modern Ho Chi Minh City, Long An, Tây Ninh, Bình Dương, Đồng Nai, Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu, Tiền Giang)

region.text: Vĩnh Long, Hà Tiên and Châu Đốc, the three western provinces of Cochinchina (the rest of the Mekong delta)

ledger.note: 1867: the French annex the western provinces. The French annexed Vĩnh Long, Hà Tiên and Châu Đốc in 1867 without resistance; the Treaty of Saigon (1874) concluded the French annexation of Cochinchina.

region.text: Northern Vietnam

ledger.note: 1883: Tonkin becomes a French protectorate. The Harmand Convention (25 August 1883, dated in the text to 25 September 1883) turned Northern Vietnam into a French protectorate; the 1883 Treaty of Huế was never ratified in France. The page gives two dates for the convention, so no month is recorded.

region.text: Annam, the central coast

ledger.note: 1884: Annam becomes a French protectorate. The Treaty of Patenôtre (6 June 1884) confirmed French dominion over Vietnam, creating the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin; the Treaty of Tientsin of 9 June 1885 ended the Sino-French War and severed the tributary relationship with Qing China.

region.text: the Nguyễn state, partitioned into the Annam and Tonkin protectorates and French Cochinchina

ledger.note: 1884: the Nguyễn state ends as a sovereign power with the Treaty of Patenôtre of 6 June 1884; the emperors reign on as figureheads, and 'all emperors after Đồng Khánh were chosen by the French' until the Empire of Vietnam ended on 25 August 1945.

wars.name: Nguyễn Ánh's war against the Tây Sơn

zones.text: the Tây Sơn heartland between Quy Nhơn and Phú Xuân (Huế)

wars.outcome: Nguyễn victory: Qui Nhơn 1799/1801, Phú Xuân 3 May 1801, Hanoi 20 July 1802; the Tây Sơn dynasty ended.
wars.note: The pages disagree on several dates: Qui Nhơn 1799 (Gia Long) vs 1800 (Tây Sơn); Hanoi 20 July (Nguyen), 22 July (Gia Long), 18 June 1802 (Tây Sơn infobox).

wars.name: Lê Văn Khôi revolt
wars.outcome: Rebels held Saigon (reduced to the citadel by late 1833) until it was recaptured in September 1835; Khôi died in December 1834.

wars.name: Siamese-Vietnamese War (1833-1834)

zones.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

wars.outcome: Vietnamese victory; Siam withdrew by April 1834 and Trấn Tây Province was set up in November 1835.

wars.name: Siamese-Vietnamese War (1841-1845)

zones.text: Cambodia outside the north-western provinces Siam ruled directly from 1794

wars.outcome: Stalemate: agreement of January 1847, Cambodia under joint suzerainty; both armies left in 1847-1848.

wars.name: Cochinchina campaign

zones.text: Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa, the three eastern provinces of Cochinchina (modern Ho Chi Minh City, Long An, Tây Ninh, Bình Dương, Đồng Nai, Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu, Tiền Giang)

wars.outcome: French victory: Saigon taken 17 February 1859; Treaty of Saigon, June 1862, cedes Gia Định, Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa.

wars.name: French conquest of Tonkin and Annam
wars.outcome: Protectorates: Harmand Convention (1883) and Treaty of Patenôtre (6 June 1884); the Sino-French War ended with the Treaty of Tientsin of 9 June 1885.

certainty.note: A conquest state in the south and a country whose highland, Lao and Cambodian frontiers were approximate; the Chinese frontier is the Qing tributary frontier.
The Cochinchina frontier follows the provinces named in the treaties of 1862 and 1867; the highland, Lao and Chinese frontiers stay soft.

notes: Cliopatria row Nguyễn dynasty 1791..1884 (11 shapes) reviewed, plus two new keyframes (1788-1790 and 1801-1802). Identity choice: the dossier starts at Nguyễn Ánh's recapture of Saigon (7 September 1788), not at Cliopatria's 1791 or the dynasty's 1802, so that 1788-1802 is drawn as the same state (the 1 June 1802 coronation is a rename); the Nguyễn lords (nguyen-lords, Cliopatria to 1775) and the Tây Sơn (tay-son-dynasty) are the neighbouring dossiers. The dossier ends in 1884 with the Treaty of Patenôtre although the emperors reigned until 1945 as figureheads. Cliopatria errors found: (1) the whole Mekong delta is removed in 1859, but the page gives steps in June 1862 and 1867 (keyframe 1859 adjusted); (2) the 1800 shape is kept until 1802 although Qui Nhơn and Phú Xuân fell in 1801 (new 1801 keyframe); (3) the 1791-1799 shapes are very small (8,428 km2 for Gia Định) and unverified for extent. Page silent or in conflict: no area is on the Nguyen page (only an 1838 administrative map), so the area comparison is not possible; Qui Nhơn 1799 or 1800; Hanoi 20 July, 22 July or 18 June 1802; Gia Định recaptured 1787 or 1788 on the Nguyen page itself; the Phú Yên advance of 1796 and the 1834 gain in Ninh Thuận (Cham principality) are dated by nothing opened; the Nguyen page says Siam seized northern Cambodia in 1814, a date the Rattanakosin page gives as 1794 for the north-west; the Nguyen page says Minh Mạng seized Savannakhet in 1827 while the Lao rebellion page gives Vietnam no military role; no page opened for this dossier dates the end of Huế's suzerainty over Cambodia (recorded at 1863, the French protectorate year given on the Rattanakosin page, confidence 1). Not covered: the Chinese tributary relation (a Qing-side vassal event, for the ea-08 Qing dossier), the Lao principalities and Muang Phuan as Vietnamese vassals, the Cham principality, the 1873 Garnier expedition and the 1874 treaty details, the Black Flags. Budget: 5 pages opened against 5. The tay-son-dynasty dossier records Nguyễn Ánh's earlier tenure of Gia Định (1778-1785) with counterpart nguyen-dynasty; this dossier starts at 1788 (Cliopatria 1791), so those earlier years have no shape here. Counterparts needing dossiers: Lê Văn Khôi's rebels (a rebel state 1833-1835, Saigon citadel), the Cham remnant (Panduranga, to 1832-1834), the Cambodian kingdom (post-angkor-cambodia): the Cliopatria 'Cambodia' row 1700-1802 is the Mekong delta, per the cambodia dossier, and it names nguyen-dynasty as its successor, which fits this dossier's 1791-1802 delta shape. Quote policy: single quotation marks enclose only wording that the WebFetch result itself gave in quotation marks; every other statement attributed to a page is a close paraphrase. Reviewer se-01-j (2026-10-19): the Cham gain is now dated November 1832 on the Champa page (added to sources), matching the champa dossier; the 1834 date above is superseded.
